items.summary: Abstract defines OpenHands as a platform for building AI agents that interact with the world like a human developer: writing code, using a command line, and browsing the web.
items.value: a platform for the development of powerful and flexible AI agents that interact with the world in similar ways to those of a human developer: by writing code, interacting with a command line, and browsing the web

items.summary: The paper lists five platform features: an event-stream interaction mechanism, a docker-sandboxed runtime with bash/browser/IPython, an interface for code+exec+browse actions, multi-agent delegation, and an evaluation framework.
items.value: (1) An interaction mechanism ... event stream architecture ... (2) A runtime environment ... docker-sandboxed operating system with a bash shell, a web browser, and IPython server ... (3) An interface allowing the agent to interact with the environment ... (4) Multi-agent delegation ... (5) Evaluation framework

items.summary: The agent's 'state' is a data structure whose key component is the event stream: a chronological list of past actions and observations, plus auxiliary bookkeeping (LLM cost, multi-agent delegation metadata).
items.value: the state is a data structure that encapsulates all relevant information for the agent's execution. A key component of this state is the event stream, which is a chronological collection of past actions and observations

items.summary: Three core action types connect an agent to the environment: IPythonRunCellAction and CmdRunAction (execute Python/bash in the sandbox) and BrowseInteractiveAction (browser DSL from BrowserGym).
items.value: Actions IPythonRunCellAction and CmdRunAction enable the agent to execute arbitrary Python code and bash commands inside the sandbox environment ... BrowserInteractiveAction enables interaction with a web browser with a domain-specific language for browsing introduced by BrowserGym (Drouin et al., 2024)

items.summary: Authors state the action set was chosen to give a comprehensive, flexible set of primitives covering most human-software-engineer tasks, and that the code/PL-based action space is powerful yet reliable and easy to maintain.
items.value: These actions were chosen to provide a comprehensive yet flexible set of primitives covering most tasks performed by human software engineers and analysts. The action space based on programming languages (PL) is powerful and flexible enough to perform any task with tools in different forms (e.g., Python function, REST API, etc.) while being reliable and easy to maintain (Wang et al., 2024a)
items.notes: rationale for the design_choice of a code-execution action space over fixed tool-calling.

items.summary: The PL-based action space is compatible with fixed tool-calling agents (users can define Python-function tools) and lets agents create their own tools by writing code when no ready-made API exists.
items.value: This design is also compatible with existing tool-calling agents that require a list of pre-defined tools (Chase, 2022) ... the framework's powerful PL-based primitives further make it possible for the agents to create tools by themselves (e.g., by generating Python functions, Yuan et al. 2023) when API to complete the task is unavailable

items.summary: The Agent Runtime gives agents a bash terminal, a Jupyter notebook for on-the-fly code execution, and a web browser, comparable to a human developer's toolset.
items.value: It allows the agent to access a bash terminal to run code and command line tools, utilize a Jupyter notebook for writing and executing code on-the-fly, and interact with a web browser for web-based tasks

items.summary: For every task session OpenHands starts an isolated Docker container; the framework talks to it over a REST action-execution API and mounts a configurable workspace directory into the sandbox.
items.value: For each task session, OpenHands spins up a securely isolated docker container sandbox, where all the actions from the event stream are executed ... A configurable workspace directory containing files the user wants the agent to work on is mounted into that secure sandbox

items.summary: The introduction frames the motivating design question of ensuring agent-driven software development is safe and avoids negative side effects on the user's system.
items.value: How can we ensure that development is safe and avoids negative side effects on the users' systems?
items.notes: motivation cited as the reason for sandboxed/isolated execution (E009).

items.summary: Inside the sandbox, the OpenHands Action Execution API runs a bash shell, a Jupyter IPython server, and a Playwright-based Chromium browser exposing BrowserGym action primitives; browser observations include HTML, DOM, accessibility tree, screenshot, and open tabs.
items.value: (1) A bash shell ... (2) A Jupyter IPython server ... (3) A Chromium browser based on Playwright. The provider provides a set of action primitives defined by BrowserGym (ServiceNow; Drouin et al., 2024) ... the browser runtime provides a rich set of observations about the current state of the browser, including HTML, DOM, accessibility tree (Mozilla), screenshot, opened tabs, etc.

items.summary: OpenHands can build its runtime on top of any user-provided base Docker image, installing its action-execution API into that image.
items.value: OpenHands allows agents to run on arbitrary operating systems with different software environments by supporting runtime based on arbitrary docker images. OpenHands implements a build mechanism that takes a user-provided arbitrary docker image and installs OpenHands action execution API into that image

items.summary: Authors motivate the AgentSkills library by citing SWE-Agent's finding that a carefully crafted agent-computer interface (ACI) matters, while noting that building/maintaining/distributing many tools across agent implementations is a hard engineering problem.
items.value: SWE-Agent (Yang et al., 2024) highlights the importance of a carefully crafted Agent-Computer Interface (ACI, i.e., specialized tools for particular tasks) in successfully solving complex tasks. However, creating, maintaining, and distributing a wide array of tools can be a daunting engineering challenge, especially when we want to make these tools available to different agent implementations
items.notes: motivation for building a shared AgentSkills library.

items.summary: AgentSkills has an explicit inclusion criterion: a skill is added only if the LLM cannot already write the code directly, or the skill needs to call an external model.
items.value: In the AgentSkills library, we do not aim to wrap every possible Python package and re-teach agents their usage ... We only add a new skill when: (1) it is not readily achievable for LLM to write code directly (e.g., edit code and replace certain lines), and/or (2) it involves calling an external model
items.notes: design_choice rationale for what belongs in AgentSkills.

items.summary: AgentSkills includes file-editing utilities (e.g., edit_file, scroll_up/scroll_down adapted from SWE-Agent and Aider) and multi-modal document readers (parse_pdf, parse_image, parse_docx, parse_audio, parse_video, parse_pptx) auto-imported into the IPython environment.
items.value: AgentSkills library includes file editing utilities adapted from SWE-Agent (Yang et al., 2024) and Aider (Gauthier) like edit_file ... scrolling functions scroll_up and scroll_down ... tools that support reading multi-modal documents, like parse_image and parse_pdf

items.summary: A dedicated action, AgentDelegateAction, lets one agent hand off a subtask to another agent; e.g. the generalist CodeActAgent delegates web-browsing subtasks to the specialized BrowsingAgent.
items.value: we use a special action type AgentDelegateAction, which enables an agent to delegate a specific subtask to another agent. For example, the generalist CodeActAgent, with limited support for web-browsing, can use AgentDelegateAction to delegate web browsing tasks to the specialized BrowsingAgent
items.notes: also functions as design-choice rationale for why delegation exists.

items.summary: CodeActAgent is the default generalist agent (CodeAct framework); at each step it can converse or act by executing bash/Python/browser code; v1.5+ can edit files, browse, and run programs.
items.value: CodeActAgent is the default generalist agent based on the CodeAct framework (Wang et al., 2024a). At each step, the agent can (1) converse ... or (2) to perform the task by executing code ... This general action space allows the agent (v1.5 and above) to perform various tasks, including editing files, browsing the web, running programs

items.summary: Browsing Agent is a generalist baseline web agent similar to WebArena's own agent, with improved observations/actions, using only zero-shot prompting.
items.value: We implemented a generalist web agent called Browsing Agent, to serve as a simple yet effective baseline for web agent tasks. The agent is similar to that in WebArena (Zhou et al., 2023a), but with improved observations and actions, with only zero-shot prompting

items.summary: GPTSwarm is integrated as an agent: it represents agent systems as optimizable graphs (nodes = operations, edges = collaboration/communication) enabling automatic optimization of multi-agent systems.
items.value: GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., 2024) pioneers the use of optimizable graphs to construct agent systems ... Each node represents a distinct operation, while edges define collaboration and communication pathways. This design allows automatic optimization of nodes and edges

items.summary: Micro agents reuse a generalist agent's implementation but specialize toward one task; authors state the goal is to lower the barrier to agent development so community members can share task-specific prompts.
items.value: OpenHands enables the creation of micro agent, an agent specialized towards a particular task. A micro agent re-uses most implementations from an existing generalist agent ... It is designed to lower the barrier to agent development, where community members can share specialized prompts that work well for their particular use cases

items.summary: Table 1 compares 12 agent frameworks (incl. OpenHands) on 9 dimensions (GUI, tool library, sandbox, browser, multi-agent, human-AI collaboration, AgentHub, evaluation framework, agent QC); the paper's own text extraction lost the checkmark/x grid, leaving only framework names, the domain column, and column headers.
items.value: Frameworks listed: AutoGPT, LangChain, MetaGPT, AutoGen, AutoAgents, Agents, Xagents, OpenAgents, GPTSwarm, AutoCodeRover, SWE-Agent, OpenHands. Columns: Domain, Graphic User Interface, Standardized Tool Library, Built-in Sandbox & Code Execution, Built-in Web Browser, Multi-agent Collaboration, Human-AI Collaboration, AgentHub, Evaluation Framework, Agent QC.
items.notes: Comparison grid values (which framework has which capability) did not survive text extraction; see missing_evidence.json. Only the qualitative statements in the Related Work appendix (E022-E027) can be used to characterize other frameworks.

items.summary: Related work: LangChain and LangGraph provide foundational building blocks with basic runtime support.
items.value: LangChain and LangGraph Chase (2022) provide foundational building blocks with basic runtime support

items.summary: Related work: CrewAI focuses on orchestrating multi-agent communications and offers a sandboxed but limited code-interpreter feature.
items.value: CrewAI CrewAI (2024) focuses on orchestrating multi-agent communications ... frameworks like CrewAI offer sandboxed but limited code interpreter features

items.summary: Related work: BrowserGym specifically targets web-browsing capabilities.
items.value: BrowserGym ServiceNow specifically targets web browsing capabilities

items.summary: Related work: DSPy emphasizes end-to-end prompt optimization.
items.value: DSPy Khattab et al. (2024) emphasizes end-to-end prompt optimization

items.summary: Related work: AutoGen implements Python and bash execution but with stateless command execution.
items.value: AutoGen Wu et al. (2023) advances beyond basic frameworks by implementing Python and bash execution capabilities, though with stateless command execution

items.summary: Related work: software-engineering-specific frameworks each cover one slice -- ChatDev automates the dev lifecycle like a waterfall model, AutoCodeRover fixes issues via code search + AST manipulation, AgentCoder iterates code generation with integrated testing, SWE-Agent integrates LLMs for automated GitHub-issue fixing.
items.value: ChatDev Qian et al. (2023) automate the software development lifecycle akin to the waterfall model, and AutoCodeRover Zhang et al. (2024b) addresses GitHub issues via code search and abstract syntax tree manipulation. AgentCoder Huang et al. (2024) iteratively refines code generation with integrated testing and feedback, while SWE-Agent Yang et al. (2024) integrates LLMs for automated Github issue fixing, streamlining software engineering

items.summary: OpenHands ships a chat-based GUI that visualizes agent actions in real time and lets the user interrupt the agent at any moment to give feedback.
items.value: OpenHands features a rich graphical user interface that visualizes the agent's current actions ... The user may interrupt the agent at any moment to provide additional feedback, comments, or instruction while the agent is working

items.summary: OpenHands' integration-test framework intercepts every LLM call and replays cached, exact-match prompt/response pairs, explicitly to solve LLM non-determinism and to cut evaluation cost; tests run on every PR/commit across multiple OSes and sandbox types.
items.value: Addressing the challenge of non-determinism in large language models (LLMs) and the associated high costs, the framework intercepts all LLM calls and supplies predefined responses based on exact prompt matches ... Tests are automatically scheduled for every pull request and commit on the main branch, running across multiple platforms, environments, and agents, including Linux and Mac, and in local, SSH, and exec sandboxes
items.notes: design_choice rationale for the Agent QC / integration-test framework.

items.summary: Running a full SWE-Bench Lite evaluation with gpt-4o costs about $600 (footnote, motivating the mocked-LLM integration-test framework).
items.value: Running a SWE-Bench Lite Jimenez et al. (2024) evaluation with gpt-4o costs around 600 USD

items.summary: The paper explains it defaults to the SWE-Bench Lite subset (not the full 2294-instance set) for cost-saving reasons, and reports all SWE-Bench results without the benchmark's optional natural-language hint text.
items.value: A canonical subset, SWE-bench Lite, is created to facilitate accessible and efficient testing. We default to use this subset for testing for cost-saving consideration ... Throughout this paper, we report all results without using hint text

items.summary: Running the complete SWE-Bench (2294 instances) is estimated at $6.9k, using a conservative $3-per-instance estimate.
items.value: Running the complete set of 2294 instances costs $6.9k, using a conservative estimate of $3 per instance

items.summary: The authors motivate using software/code execution as the agent-environment interface: software is one of humans' most powerful tools for acting on the world, and existing software tooling makes it 'the ideal interface for AI agents to interact with the world in complex ways.'
items.value: The most powerful way in which humans currently interact with the world is through software ... Given the power of software, as well as the existing tooling around its efficient development, use, and deployment, it provides the ideal interface for AI agents to interact with the world in complex ways
items.notes: motivation for the whole platform's design (software-as-interface).

items.summary: The authors note that their HumanEvalFix comparison to SWE-Agent is not matched: SWE-Agent was given a full one-shot demonstration trajectory, while OpenHands was evaluated zero-shot.
items.value: While SWE-Agent achieves 87.7%, Yang et al. (2024) provides the model a full demonstration of a successful sample trajectory fixing one of the bugs in the test dataset ("1-shot"), whereas our evaluation of OpenHands is 0-shot

items.summary: SWE-Bench Lite (300 instances, no hint text) resolve rates for non-OpenHands agent baselines: SWE-Agent 18.0%, AutoCodeRover 19.0%, Aider 26.3%, Moatless Tools 26.7%, Agentless 27.3%.

HumanEvalFix (164 Python instances) pass rates: BLOOMZ-176B 16.6%, OctoCoder-15B 30.4%, DeepSeekCoder-33B-Instruct 47.5%, StarCoder2-15B 48.6%, SWE-Agent (1-shot) 87.7%, OH CodeActAgent v1.5 (0-shot) 20.1% with gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613 and 79.3% with gpt-4o-2024-05-13.

items.summary: WebArena (812 instances) success rates: Lemur 5.3%, Patel-et-al.-2024 trained-72B 9.4%, AutoWebGLM trained-7B 18.2%, Auto Eval & Refine 20.2%; WebArena Agent 6.2% (gpt-3.5-turbo) / 14.4% (gpt-4-turbo); OH BrowsingAgent v1.0: 8.5%/14.8%/15.5% (gpt-4o-mini/gpt-4o/claude-3.5-sonnet); OH CodeActAgent v1.8 via delegation to BrowsingAgent v1.0: 8.3%/14.5%/15.3% (same three models).

OH CodeActAgent v1.8 (delegation to BrowsingAgent v1.0)

items.summary: Authors' own reading of the WebArena result: their BrowsingAgent is competitive among agents that use LLMs with only domain-general prompting (as opposed to trained/specialist methods).
items.value: we can see that our BrowsingAgent achieves competitive performance among agents that use LLMs with domain-general prompting techniques

items.summary: On MiniWoB++ (125 environments), OpenHands' best configuration (BrowsingAgent v1.0 + gpt-4o, 40.8%) trails the specialist CC-Net baseline (trained with RL plus human-annotated behavioral cloning, 91.1%) by a wide margin.

value.note: trained specialist model with environment exploration
trained specialist model with RL and human-annotated behavioral cloning

value.agent: OH CodeActAgent v1.8 (delegation to BrowsingAgent v1.0)

items.notes: Classified as a negative result relative to the paper's own cross-category-competitiveness claim: a trained, task-specific reinforcement-learning system clearly outperforms every LLM-prompted agent shown, OpenHands included.

items.summary: MiniWoB++ description: 125 synthetically initialized minimalist web interfaces; easier and shorter-horizon than WebArena, with step-by-step directions; some environments need vision; the paper reports the full-set score.
items.value: The tasks are synthetically initialized on 125 different minimalist web interfaces. Unlike WebArena, tasks are easier without page changes, require fewer steps, and provide low-level step-by-step task directions ... we report the performance on the full set and only include baselines that are evaluated on the full set

items.summary: WebArena description: a self-hostable, execution-based web-agent benchmark with 812 human-curated task instructions across shopping, forums, developer platforms, and content-management systems.
items.value: WebArena comprises 812 human-curated task instructions across various domains, including shopping, forums, developer platforms, and content management systems

items.summary: GAIA (L1 validation set, 53 instances): AutoGPT+gpt-4-turbo 13.2%; OH GPTSwarm v1.0 30.2% (gpt-4-0125-preview) and 32.1% (gpt-4o-2024-05-13).

GAIA description: 466 curated real-world tasks across three difficulty levels requiring reasoning, multi-modal understanding, web browsing, and coding; OpenHands' infrastructure simplifies integrating the needed tools.
items.value: GAIA consists of 466 curated tasks across three levels ... Setting up GAIA is traditionally challenging due to the complexity of integrating various tools with the agent, but OpenHands's infrastructure ... simplifies the integration significantly

items.summary: GPQA diamond set (198 instances): expert human 81.3%, non-expert human 21.9%, few-shot chain-of-thought 29.6% (gpt-3.5-turbo-16k) / 38.8% (gpt-4), OH CodeActAgent v1.8 + claude-3-5-sonnet 52.0%.
GPQA description: graduate-level, 'Google-proof' Q&A requiring coordinated tool use; python execution and web search help with calculation and out-of-parametric-knowledge information.
items.value: GPQA (Rein et al., 2023) evaluates agents' ability for coordinated tool use when solving challenging graduate-level problems. Tool use (e.g., python) and web search are often useful

items.summary: AgentBench OS (bash) subset (144 instances): baseline agent 42.4% (gpt-4) / 32.6% (gpt-3.5-turbo); OH CodeActAgent v1.5 57.6% (gpt-4o) / 11.8% (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125).
AgentBench description: multi-turn, open-ended reasoning/decision-making; the OS (bash) subset requires agents to interact directly with a task-specific operating system via bash commands.
items.value: AgentBench (Liu et al., 2023) evaluates agents' reasoning and decision-making abilities in a multi-turn, open-ended generation setting. We selected the code-grounded operating system (OS) subset with 144 tasks

items.summary: MINT math subset (225 instances): baseline agent 65.8% (gpt-4-0613); OH CodeActAgent v1.5 77.3% (gpt-4o) / 33.8% (gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613).
MINT code subset (136 instances): OH CodeActAgent v1.5 + gpt-4o scores 50.0%, below the MINT baseline agent's 59.6% (gpt-4-0613); with gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613 OpenHands scores only 5.2%.
items.notes: Classified as a negative result: on this subset OpenHands' best backbone (gpt-4o) trails the MINT baseline agent (gpt-4-0613), unlike the pattern on most other benchmarks.

items.summary: MINT description: tests multi-turn tool use with natural-language feedback simulated by GPT-4; up to five interaction rounds with two chances to propose a solution; math/code subsets follow Yuan et al. (2024).
items.value: MINT (Wang et al., 2024b) is a benchmark designed to evaluate agents' ability to solve challenging tasks through multi-turn interactions using tools and natural language feedback simulated by GPT-4 ... we allow the agent to interact with up to five iterations with two chances to propose solutions

items.summary: ProofWriter (600 instances, 5-hop): few-shot CoT 68.1% (gpt-4); Logic-LM (gpt-4 + symbolic solver) 79.6%; OH CodeActAgent v1.5 + gpt-4o 78.8%.

ProofWriter description: a synthetic deductive-reasoning dataset; the paper focuses on the hardest 5-hop subset (600 instances) and reuses Logic-LM's logical-form parses to reduce semantic-parsing error.
items.value: ProofWriter (Tafjord et al., 2021) is a synthetic dataset created to assess deductive reasoning abilities of LLMs ... we focus on the most challenging subset, which contains 600 instances requiring 5-hop reasoning. To minimize the impact of potential errors in semantic parsing, we use the logical forms provided by Logic-LM

items.summary: Entity Deduction Arena (200 instances, average of 'Things' and 'Celebrities'): zero-shot prompting 40.0% (gpt-4-0314) / 27.0% (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613); OH CodeActAgent v1.5 38.0% (gpt-4o) / 24.0% (gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613).
items.conditions: Entity Deduction Arena, 200 instances (avg. of 'Things' and 'Celebrities')

items.summary: Entity Deduction Arena description: agents deduce an unknown entity via strategic yes/no-style questioning (a 20-Questions-like game), testing state tracking, planning, and inductive reasoning over a multi-turn dialogue.
items.value: Entity Deduction Arena (EDA) (Zhang et al., 2024a) evaluates agents' ability to deduce unknown entities through strategic questioning, akin to the 20 Questions game

items.summary: Authors' own synthesis: the same CodeAct agent, without any modification to its system prompt, is competitive across three very different task categories (software, web, misc.), which they contrast with baseline agents that are typically built and tuned for one category.
items.value: the same CodeAct agent, without any modifications to its system prompt, demonstrates competitive performance across three major task categories: software development, web interaction, and miscellaneous tasks. This is particularly significant when compared to the baseline agents, which are typically designed and optimized for specific task categories

items.summary: Table 2 lists all 15 integrated benchmarks by category (7 software, 2 web, 6 misc.) with a one-line required capability each, e.g. BIRD (text-to-SQL), BioCoder (bioinformatics coding), ML-Bench (ML-repository coding), Gorilla APIBench (API calling), ToolQA (tool use).
items.value: Software: SWE-Bench, HumanEvalFix, BIRD, BioCoder, ML-Bench, Gorilla APIBench, ToolQA. Web: WebArena, MiniWoB++. Misc. Assistance: GAIA, GPQA, AgentBench, MINT, Entity Deduction Arena, ProofWriter.
items.notes: Used to state benchmark coverage/counts; BIRD, BioCoder, ML-Bench, and Gorilla APIBench, ToolQA scores are not cited individually in the draft because their source table (Table 4) suffered column-flattening extraction damage (see missing_evidence.json).

items.summary: OpenHands is released under the MIT license, with 32K GitHub stars and more than 2.1K contributions from over 188 contributors (as of writing).
items.value: Released under a permissive MIT license allowing commercial use ... OpenHands has gained significant traction, with 32K GitHub stars and more than 2.1K contributions from over 188 contributors

items.summary: At the time of writing, OpenHands' agent hub includes more than 10 implemented agents.
items.value: As of this writing, OpenHands includes an agent hub with over 10 implemented agents

items.summary: Authors concede multi-modality is not yet supported 'in a principled way': current file-format coverage comes only from predefined skills, not standard IPython/browser integration with vision-language models.
items.value: Enhanced multi-modality support. While our current implementation already supports a wide range of file formats through predefined agent skills, we are interested in enabling multi-modality in a principled way through standard IPython and browser integration, such as viewing images and videos using vision-language model through a browser or processing XLSX files with code

items.summary: Broad author concession: current agents still struggle with complex tasks; the authors want to improve agents via both training and inference-time techniques.
items.value: Stronger agents. Current agents still struggle with complex tasks, and we are interested in building better agents through both training and inference time techniques

items.summary: Authors concede the current agent 'suffers a lot' when editing long files, and want better file-editing approaches.
items.value: Agent editing improvements. Current agent suffers a lot when editing long files, and we are interested in exploring different approaches to improve the file editing performance of agents

items.summary: Because the architecture is extensible, the authors plan to attach an optional retry/self-correction component (Auto Eval & Refine, using Reflexion-style prompts and a completion reward model) to the browsing agent in a future version.
items.value: thanks to OpenHands's extensible architecture, Auto Eval & Refine Pan et al. (2024), an agent retry-on-error strategy with Reflexion Shinn et al. (2024) prompts and task completion reward models, will be integrated as an optional component attached to our browsing agent

items.summary: Authors concede OpenHands' own workflow construction still needs substantial handcrafted work, and point to graph-based frameworks (GPTSwarm, LangGraph) as possible routes to automatic workflow generation.
items.value: Automatic workflow generation. Currently, OpenHands's workflow still requires a substantial handcrafted workload. We believe that graph-based frameworks such as GPTSwarm Zhuge et al. (2024) and LangGraph Chase (2022) could serve as alternative solutions for building agents

items.summary: Ethics statement: the authors argue OpenHands mitigates AI-agent risk by enabling systematic evaluation before wide deployment, by keeping a human in the loop rather than fully autonomous operation, and by giving safety researchers access to strong agent baselines.
items.value: OpenHands helps mitigate risks by: (1) Enabling systematic evaluation of these agents ... (2) Facilitating human-agent interaction rather than allowing agents to operate autonomously without oversight. (3) ... we hope OpenHands allows researchers worldwide to access the best suites of agents to conduct frontier safety research

items.summary: The current 'OpenHands Benchmarks' repository is migrating from the original OpenHands V0 benchmark code to the newer 'OpenHands Software Agent SDK' (V1) infrastructure; actively maintained benchmarks now listed are SWE-Bench, SWE-Bench Pro, GAIA, Commit0, OpenAgentSafety, and ProgramBench.
items.value: We are currently migrating the benchmarks from OpenHands V0 to work with the OpenHands Software Agent SDK infrastructure in V1 ... Available Benchmarks: SWE-Bench, SWE-Bench Pro, GAIA, Commit0, OpenAgentSafety, ProgramBench (all Active)

items.summary: The benchmarks repo now supports remote, massively parallel evaluation (32+ concurrent workers) and ties compatibility between the benchmarks code and the SDK to specific commits (e.g., an SDK 'critic' module introduced at commit 79868ae5, 17 Nov 2025, creates a version boundary).
items.value: allowing for massive parallelization (e.g., 32+ concurrent workers) ... As of SDK commit 79868ae5 (November 17, 2025), the OpenHands Agent SDK introduced the openhands.sdk.critic module. Current benchmarks code imports CriticBase from this module

items.summary: The project now also ships 'Agent Canvas', described as a self-hosted developer control center that can run OpenHands' own agent or third-party agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, or any Agent-Client-Protocol-compatible agent) across local, remote, or cloud backends, and wire them into automations (Slack, GitHub, Linear, etc.).
items.value: OpenHands Agent Canvas turns your coding agents into a self-hosted, always-on engineering team ... Run OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, or any ACP-compatible agent across local, remote, and cloud backends

items.summary: The project is now organized as a multi-repository system: OpenHands/OpenHands (Agent Canvas frontend and local-stack orchestration), software-agent-sdk (Python SDK, Agent Server, canonical server API), typescript-client (browser client), and automation (scheduling, webhooks, run history).

items.summary: Conclusion (verbatim): OpenHands is presented as a community-driven platform enabling agents that interact with the world through software, via an interaction mechanism, a safe sandbox, agent skills, multi-agent collaboration, and an evaluation framework.
items.value: We introduce OpenHands, a community-driven platform that enables the development of agents that interact with the world through software interfaces. By providing a powerful interaction mechanism, a safe sandboxed environment, essential agent skills, multi-agent collaboration capabilities, and a comprehensive evaluation framework, OpenHands accelerates research innovations and real-world applications of agentic AI systems
